name: Snowflake
summary: A fully managed cloud data warehouse that separates storage from compute, with virtual warehouses billed per second.
intro: Snowflake stores tables in its own compressed, columnar format, split into micro-partitions in cloud object storage. Compute comes from virtual warehouses: clusters you size from X-Small (1 credit per hour) to 6X-Large (512 credits per hour), each size double the one before. Warehouses don’t share compute, so a loading job never slows a dashboard. They suspend when idle and resume on the next query, billed per second with a 60-second minimum each time one starts.

A cloud services layer handles metadata, query parsing and optimisation, and security, and Snowflake runs on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. It also manages Apache Iceberg tables: data and metadata sit in your own bucket (an external volume), Snowflake either acts as the catalog or connects to an external Iceberg REST catalog, and it supports Iceberg spec versions 1, 2 and 3. Snowflake Open Catalog is a managed service for Apache Polaris, an open-source Iceberg REST catalog.
strengths: Very little to tune: no physical design, storage grooming or nodes to manage
A separate warehouse per workload, each sized, scaled and suspended on its own
Zero-copy cloning and data sharing between accounts
Iceberg tables let other engines that speak the Iceberg REST protocol work on the same data without exports
limits: Proprietary and billed in credits; costs grow with warehouse size and running time
Snowflake manages how native tables are stored, in its own internal format; for files other engines can read, use Iceberg tables in your own storage
Each warehouse start is billed for at least 60 seconds, so frequent suspends and resumes for short queries add up
Standard tables are built for analytics; fast single-row reads and writes need hybrid tables, a separate row-based table type

story: By the early 2010s, traditional data warehouses ran on small, static clusters of machines. They depended on deep ETL pipelines and careful physical tuning, and they struggled with the schema-less JSON arriving from logs, web and mobile apps. Hadoop and Spark could process anything, but lacked much of a warehouse’s efficiency and features and took significant engineering effort to roll out. Meanwhile, public clouds offered almost unlimited compute and storage on demand, which warehouses built for fixed resources couldn’t use.

In July 2012, Benoît Dageville and Thierry Cruanes, database architects at Oracle, and Marcin Żukowski, a co-founder of the Vectorwise analytical database, founded Snowflake Computing, with Mike Speiser of Sutter Hill Ventures as its first CEO. Implementation began in late 2012. Rather than build on Hadoop or PostgreSQL, they wrote the engine from scratch for the cloud. Snowflake unveiled its service in October 2014 and became generally available on AWS in June 2015.

Snowflake made the warehouse a pure service with no tuning knobs and no hardware to buy, with storage and compute scaling separately. At its September 2020 IPO it sold 28 million shares at $120 each, raising about $3.4 billion.

choices.why: In shared-nothing warehouses each node owns a slice of the data, so resizing or losing a node means reshuffling data, and loading and querying compete for the same hardware. Snowflake keeps one copy of the data and runs separate compute clusters (virtual warehouses) against it.

choices.choice: Store tables in S3 instead of building a storage layer
choices.why: The team experimented and found S3’s availability and durability hard to beat, even with variable performance. They put their effort into local caching in the compute layer instead of writing their own HDFS-like service.

choices.choice: A pure service with no knobs
choices.why: Users don’t buy machines, hire DBAs or install software, and there is no physical design or storage grooming to do. That was meant to bring a warehouse to teams that couldn’t afford the cost and complexity of traditional ones.

choices.choice: Semi-structured data as a first-class type
choices.why: More and more data came from logs, web and mobile apps as JSON and similar formats. Built-in SQL extensions let users load and query it without first designing a schema and ETL pipeline.
